extracted.intended_audience: aspiring stand-up comedians, comedy writers, and students of joke craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting and performing concise, witty one-liners in stand-up comedy, focusing on structure, wordplay, persona, and delivery (deadpan).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: One-liners are short and to the point, often delivering the punchline immediately without much buildup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the line concise so the punchline lands immediately. Examples on the page: 'I spilled spot remover on my dog, now he’s gone.' and 'If at first you don’t succeed, then skydiving isn’t for you.' Avoid unnecessary setup or extra clauses that dilute the instant payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleverness (wordplay and surprise)
rubrics_metrics.description: One-liners rely on clever wordplay, double meanings, or unexpected twists to create humor; humor is often derived from a clever observation about everyday life or a surprising connection between ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use puns, semantic ambiguity, and lateral associations to create the twist. Examples: 'What’s another word for Thesaurus?' and 'If you saw a heat wave, would you wave back?' Aim for an economy that reveals the twist in a single line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format (single-sentence structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: One-liners are structured as a single sentence or line, which contrasts with jokes that may involve a setup and punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose the joke so it reads and performs as a single unit. This enforces economy and forces the writer to embed setup and payoff in the same sentence. The page contrasts this with longer jokes and riddles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directness (immediate reaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: One-liners aim for an immediate laugh or reaction, often relying on the audience’s quick recognition of the humor or irony present in the statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clarity so audiences can instantly process the incongruity or wordplay. Avoid ambiguities that require long explanation; the success metric is an immediate audible reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-setup economy (joke without explicit setup)
rubrics_metrics.description: One-liners achieve the joke without a separate setup and punchline; the joke must be self-contained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed context and payoff tightly. The author notes Steven Wright occasionally uses a set-up/punchline but excels at one-line non-sequiturs; know when an exception is justified but default to self-contained lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idiom/cliché subversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of Wright’s earlier jokes were derived from taking an idiom or cliché and reforming the ending.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with familiar phrases or clichés and twist the expected ending to produce surprise (example: 'It’s a small world, I wouldn’t want to have to paint it.'). Watch for predictability—subversions should feel fresh, not rote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan persona / staying in the bit
rubrics_metrics.description: Delivery should maintain a consistent deadpan persona: do not look to the audience for approval; remain in a state described as bewilderment, frustration, and confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform with a flat affect and avoid audience-seeking smiles or nods. Jerry Seinfeld’s phrase 'staying in the bit' is cited—remain character-consistent to amplify the incongruity and create a subtle mystery around the performer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend of character and material to create mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine the writing with a stable onstage character (Wright’s bewildered/confused persona) so the lines build a persona-driven world that adds depth to the one-liners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use delivery and repeated character cues to make lines feel part of a coherent persona, which can magnify otherwise short non-sequiturs. The page recommends watching video to see how Wright blends his deadpan character with material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observational and non-sequitur style
rubrics_metrics.description: Many successful one-liners are observational or non-sequiturs: sharp, often absurd observations about everyday life that take an unexpected turn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor lines that isolate a tiny observation and then deliver a surreal or logically odd conclusion (examples: 'Curiosity killed the cat, but for a while I was a suspect.' and 'I watched the Indy 500 and I was thinking if they left earlier, they wouldn’t have to go so fast.'). Maintain internal logic to the absurdity so the surprise feels earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleanliness / audience appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Wright’s observations are described as 'poignant, clever and always clean,' implying a value on content that avoids graphic or offensive material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider keeping material broadly clean to increase accessibility and longevity; cleanliness is presented as a stylistic choice that suited Wright’s persona and widened his appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and video study
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the lines alongside performance video to observe timing, pauses, facial expression, and how persona affects delivery; the author embedded a compilation video for this purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t evaluate one-liners solely on the page; watch performances to learn timing, cadence, and how tiny pauses or looks supplement a single sentence. Practice by mimicking then adapting timing to your own persona.
